c.tagline: Birthplace of America - Liberty Bell, cheesesteaks, murals, and rowhouse charm.

taxi.fareNote: Metered cabs can be hailed in Center City; elsewhere most visitors book Uber or Lyft. Airport taxis to Center City run a flat rate.

emergency.note: 911 is the single emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Kensington open-air drug market — avoid; caution in parts of North and West Philadelphia

hood_desc: The elegant, walkable heart of Philadelphia around leafy Rittenhouse Square, lined with upscale hotels, boutiques, and acclaimed restaurants; the most convenient base for first-time visitors.
The cobblestone historic district containing Independence Hall, the Liberty Bell, and Elfreth's Alley, plus art galleries and buzzing weekend bars; essential for history lovers and sightseers.

A former working-class riverside neighborhood turned national hotspot for indie music venues, craft breweries, coffee roasters, and inventive restaurants; the go-to for hip nightlife and creative energy.
The leafy academic quarter west of the Schuylkill, home to the University of Pennsylvania, Drexel, the Penn Museum, and student-friendly cafes; calm, green, and cultured.
The soul of Philadelphia's food culture, from the historic Italian Market to the BYOB restaurants and cafes of East Passyunk Avenue, near the stadium district; a dining lover's neighborhood.
lodging: Motto by Hilton Philadelphia Rittenhouse Square
Best Western Plus Independence Park Hotel
Courtyard by Marriott Philadelphia South at The Navy Yard

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink.

transit.pay: Tap a SEPTA Key card or a contactless bank card or phone at subway turnstiles and on trolleys and buses. The base fare is $2.50 and a One Day Convenience Pass is $6.50; Regional Rail fares are zone-based and higher. Key cards are reloadable and sold at stations and retailers.
transit.hours: The Broad Street and Market-Frankford subway lines run 24 hours on weekends and roughly 5am to midnight on weekdays (Owl bus service overnight); trolleys and buses vary.

train: William H. Gray III 30th Street Station (Amtrak)
bus: Intercity bus stops near 30th Street Station (Greyhound, Megabus, FlixBus)

transit.m: SEPTA Airport Line (Regional Rail) to Center City (~25 min)

tip.r: ~15-20% is standard at restaurants; round up for taxis and tip $1-2 per drink at bars.

food.name: Cheesesteak
food.desc: Thin-sliced ribeye griddled with onions on a long Italian roll, sealed with provolone, American or Cheez Whiz. Order style first, then wit or witout onions.

places.name: John's Roast Pork
places.note: Beam Award winner and the choice of locals who think the tourist corners are overrated.

places.name: Dalessandro's Steaks
places.note: Neighbourhood corner shop with finely chopped meat and a devoted North West Philly following.

places.name: Pat's King of Steaks and Geno's Steaks
places.note: The rival 24-hour corner where the sandwich was born; worth it for the theatre.

food.name: Roast Pork Sandwich
food.desc: Philadelphia's real signature - slow-roasted pork with garlicky jus, sharp provolone and bitter broccoli rabe or spinach on a seeded roll.

places.name: John's Roast Pork
places.note: Family-run since 1930 and widely called the best roast pork sandwich in the city.

places.name: Tommy DiNic's
places.note: Market counter that made the roast pork sandwich nationally famous; expect a queue at lunch.

places.name: Cosmi's Deli
places.note: Corner deli beloved by locals for roast pork and hoagies, open late.

food.name: Philly Soft Pretzel
food.desc: Figure-eight pretzels baked in joined rows, chewy and salted, torn apart and eaten with yellow mustard - a breakfast habit, not a snack.

places.name: Center City Pretzel Co.
places.note: Overnight bakery selling straight from the oven; the pretzel other bakers buy at 3am.

places.name: Miller's Twist
places.note: Hand-twisted pretzels rolled in front of you in the market; also does pretzel dogs.

places.name: Philly Pretzel Factory
places.note: Local chain born in Northeast Philly, the easy everyday option across the city.

food.name: Water Ice
food.desc: Philadelphia's summer institution - a fine, smooth fruit ice somewhere between sorbet and slush, with lemon, cherry and mango the classics.

places.name: John's Water Ice
places.note: Family-run since 1945, four classic flavours only; a South Philly summer landmark.

places.name: Pop's Homemade Italian Ice
places.note: Century-old stand still handmaking water ice and gelato each season.

places.name: Rita's Italian Ice
places.note: Philadelphia-area chain; the reliable stop for a gelati anywhere in the city.

food.name: Italian Hoagie
food.desc: A cold sub done Philly-style - Italian meats, sharp provolone, shredded lettuce, tomato, onion, oregano and oil on a crusty seeded roll.

places.name: Ricci's Hoagies
places.note: Corner hoagie shop trading since 1920, still using its own bread recipe.

places.name: Cosmi's Deli
places.note: Old-school deli counter turning out enormous hoagies until late.

places.name: Italian Market Delis, 9th Street
places.note: Historic open-air market strip of Italian delis, cheese shops and butchers.

food.name: Scrapple and a Philly Breakfast
food.desc: Pennsylvania Dutch loaf of pork scraps and cornmeal, sliced and fried crisp, eaten with eggs and often a drizzle of syrup.

places.name: Dutch Eating Place
places.note: Pennsylvania Dutch counter in the market; scrapple, pancakes and apple dumplings.

places.name: Down Home Diner
places.note: Full breakfast diner inside the market, scrapple served with eggs all morning.

places.name: Sabrina's Cafe
places.note: Popular local brunch mini-chain with a modern take on scrapple and stuffed french toast.

food.name: Philadelphia Craft Beer
food.desc: A deep beer town - Yards and Victory lead the local taps, and the city's tavern culture goes back to colonial times.

places.name: Yards Brewing Company
places.note: Big taproom of Philadelphia's best-known brewery, with tours and a kitchen.

places.name: Standard Tap
places.note: Gastropub that helped start the local-only draft movement; all-Philadelphia beer list.

places.name: Monk's Cafe
places.note: Legendary Belgian beer bar and the reason many people first came to Philly to drink.

food.name: Philly Sodas and Birch Beer
food.desc: Local soft drinks - Hank's birch beer and Frank's black cherry wishniak, both Philadelphia-made and the standard chaser to a cheesesteak.

places.name: Reading Terminal Market
places.note: Market grocers and lunch counters stock Hank's and Frank's by the bottle.

places.name: Italian Market Grocers, 9th Street
places.note: Corner grocers along the market strip sell the local sodas cold by the case.

places.name: John's Roast Pork
places.note: Serves the local bottled sodas alongside its sandwiches, as tradition demands.

landmarks: Liberty Bell
This cracked bronze bell is one of America's most powerful symbols of independence and freedom.
Independence Hall
The birthplace of the Declaration of Independence and U.S. Constitution, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Rocky Statue
The bronze statue of Rocky Balboa at the base of the Art Museum steps is a beloved pop-culture photo stop.
Philadelphia Museum of Art
This grand Greek Revival museum with its iconic 'Rocky Steps' offers a sweeping skyline backdrop and world-class art.
Philadelphia City Hall
The largest municipal building in the U.S., topped by a statue of William Penn, dominates the skyline with Second Empire grandeur.
Reading Terminal Market
A historic indoor market bursting with local food stalls, offering a sensory, photogenic slice of Philly culture.
Eastern State Penitentiary
This hauntingly beautiful, ruined Gothic prison once held Al Capone and now draws photographers to its crumbling cellblocks.
Elfreth's Alley
America's oldest continuously inhabited residential street, lined with colonial-era row homes straight out of the 18th century.
LOVE Park (Robert Indiana's LOVE sculpture)
Robert Indiana's colorful LOVE sculpture is one of the most Instagrammed spots in the city and a symbol of Philadelphia itself.
Boathouse Row
A row of Victorian-era boathouses along the Schuylkill River, famously outlined in lights at night for a stunning waterfront view.

train.note: No international trains; the nearest cross-border services are Amtrak's Adirondack and Maple Leaf out of New York. Almost everything uses William H. Gray III 30th Street Station, where Acela and Northeast Regional trains reach New York in about 1 hour 20 minutes and Washington DC in under 2 hours, Keystone Service trains run west to Lancaster and Harrisburg, and the daily Pennsylvanian continues to Pittsburgh. All 13 SEPTA Regional Rail lines call there, as does NJ Transit's Atlantic City Line. Acela fares climb steeply close to departure, so book early - Northeast Regional is far cheaper for the same city pair.

bus.note: No direct international coaches; buses to Montreal or Toronto require a change in New York. Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/), FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/), Megabus (https://us.megabus.com/) and Peter Pan (https://peterpanbus.com/) run very frequent services to New York (about 2 hours), Washington DC (3 hours), Baltimore and Pittsburgh. Since the downtown Filbert Street terminal closed, most operators use curbside stops around 30th Street Station and Market Street, so check your ticket for the exact corner. Tickets are online only for FlixBus and Megabus, and walk-up fares on the New York run can be several times the advance price.

ferry.note: The RiverLink Ferry across the Delaware from Penn's Landing to Camden is closed with no announced reopening date (https://www.delawareriverwaterfront.com/places/riverlink-ferry), so Philadelphia currently has no scheduled passenger boat service. The nearest working crossing is the Cape May-Lewes Ferry between southern New Jersey and Delaware (https://www.cmlf.com/), about two hours south by road; it takes vehicles and should be booked ahead in summer. Otherwise PATCO trains and NJ Transit's RiverLine light rail handle the Delaware River crossings.

half.name: Longwood Gardens
half.blurb: Pierre du Pont's former estate in Kennett Square, about an hour away, holds over a thousand acres of gardens, fountains and a large conservatory.

half.name: Valley Forge National Historical Park
half.blurb: Revolutionary War encampment site about 30 minutes northwest preserves log huts and cannon batteries where Washington's army wintered in 1777-78.

half.name: Lancaster County
half.blurb: Amish farmland about two hours west centers on horse-drawn buggies, farmers markets and the town of Lancaster's Central Market.

half.name: Hershey
half.blurb: Chocolate-industry town about 90 minutes northwest, built around Milton Hershey's factory, holds Hersheypark and the Hershey's Chocolate World tour.

full.name: Gettysburg
full.blurb: Civil War battlefield roughly two and a half hours west marks the site of the war's bloodiest battle and Lincoln's address.
